title: Tabitha and the Singing Glitter
markdown:
Witch Tabitha’s cottage sat wonky on a hill that sighed whenever the wind asked, as if the building and the weather had an old arrangement. Slate roofs shone after rain, a thousand fish scales. Paths to her door got lost in mountain mist on purpose and then, sheepish, found the step again. Inside: clutter with a degree—jars bubbling colours that had not consulted one another, spellbooks in wobbly stacks, a mortar that remembered more secrets than Tabitha admitted, air humming the polite sort of magic. Ink, a newt the colour of midnight velvet, sunned on the hearth stone and judged the flames. When he glowed faint blue, spells behaved. When he did not, Tabitha put the kettle on and waited.

A blustery afternoon rattled the panes. Pixie-mail zipped through the window, a tiny bell, and thumped the workbench, scattering lavender. The note was dandelion fluff, spidery urgent: Parcel delivery. Super important. Before moonrise. The Whispering Peaks Council. Tabitha’s spectacles slid. Ink flicked a tail that meant: careful, then. From a camphor chest she took a velvet-wrapped packet, ribbon like a captured moonbeam, strangely light.

“A wink’s speed,” she told him, tucking it snug in leather. Ridgeback Path hugged the mountainside; gravel crunched; valleys opened like opinions. Merry whistling, then Elf Thistle from the moss, green tunic among gnarled trees, ears twitching.

“Adventure? Watch Mayor Bumble’s latest Improvement. A sight.”

Tabitha’s sigh was dry leaves. Bumble’s improvements rarely improved.

“Town square needed sparkle. A giant glitter statue of himself, smack on the only road to the old bridge. Signs—huge, shiny—Mayor’s Magnificent Marvel. You trip over proclamations.”

Ink shimmered blue, a silent verdict on silliness.

The valley agreed with Thistle, and then some. Children had already begun to circle the statue as if it were a maypole that had got ideas. Gold glitter from boots to oversized hat, arms hugging an ego that had applied for planning permission. Signs shouted in letters you could trip over; one proclaimed MAGNIFICENT twice, in case the first had been modest. Carts had backed up. A baker argued with a sign about right of way. The hidden path they needed was a rumour behind a puddle of sparkle. Sun sank; colours argued in the clouds. The parcel felt heavier, as important things do when roads become exhibitions. Moonrise cast long appointments. Tabitha counted the hours on her fingers and disliked the sum.

“A statement,” Tabitha murmured, “not the one he meant.” Too big to move, too flashy to ignore. She knelt. “A way through without his usual fuss.”

Ink wriggled to wild thyme at the statue’s base. She picked sprigs. Then she looked at the dazzle, boot to hat.

“Thistle. More of that crinkly pixie-mail paper?”

He produced a sheet. She rubbed thyme—mint-sweet—tore paper, sprinkled. Ink glowed encouragement.

“Your very particular thing.”

Ink gathered himself with the dignity of a small dragon and sweated: not ordinary damp, a shimmering mist with an inner light, the secret he kept for glitter and emergencies. On gold dust it had a habit. The statue hummed, a pleasant cellar note, then tinkled like fairy bells that had not been invited, then chimed as if each flake had found a voice and a choir and a slightly silly hymn. Melody filled the valley, joyous, undignified, impossible to make a speech over. Windows opened. Doors forgot they were shut. A dog sat down to listen. Even Mayor Bumble stood mesmerised by his own sparkle learning music, mouth open on a proclamation that would have to wait.

They slipped the barely-there path behind the symphony to the bridge. Professor Hoot, stern owl of the Council, waited.

“Just in time.” He took the parcel. “Ingredients for Night-Blooming Serenity tea. The town needs it after the Mayor’s enthusiastic announcement. Peace. After fuss.”

The singing faded on cue. Bumble, confused by quiet, glimpsed Tabitha and Ink rounding the bend. “Where—? And what was that lovely peculiar sound?”

Glitter settled, a little less dazzling.

Home, the wonky cottage received them like a cup. Tabitha poured the newly delivered tea and found it tasted of night flowers and the particular relief of a deadline met. Ink sat on her shoulder and purred, which newts do not, except this one. Next morning she walked the ridge for the view: the signs still stood, slightly embarrassed; the statue had gone plain overnight, stone remembering it was stone. Bumble, who had slept like a log on Serenity, chuckled at the memory and admitted to Hoot, sheepish, that a little quiet might beat fuss and sparkle. A cart got through to the bridge. Tabitha watched mist curl the cottage and did not make a speech. She topped up Ink’s stone. The parcel had arrived. The town, for one morning, remembered volume.
characters: Tabitha (witch Tabitha), Ink (newt Ink), Thistle (elf Thistle)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for independent readers
